newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Lion Nathan first half profit slumps.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Lion Nathan first half profit slumps.

text.p: Australasian brewer Lion Nathan Ltd said on Monday it was confident of a better second half result after reporting a 21 percent earnings slump to NZ$72.2 million (US$50 million).
Chief executive Douglas Myers said the decline reflected very competitive markets in Australia and New Zealand and a slightly higher tax rate in the six months to February.
He also blamed anti drink-drive campaigns, decreased discretionary spending brought on by the growth in gambling on both sides of the Tasman, and a poor summer in Auckland.
"In this uncertain environment, Lion is continuing to invest in key brands to grow volume, and investing in new products and packaging," he said.

Myers also said a more centralised management structure, marrying the interests of its five regional brewing interests in Australia, would pay dividends under the stewardship of new manager Gordon Cairns.
But he acknowledged at a news conference that, with hindsight, the company should have moved two or three years earlier in reorganising its Australian operations.
These represent over 70 percent of its assets and have suffered market share losses in recent years.
Annualised Australian market share was 41.1 percent by the end of February against 42 percent six months earlier, but Myers said data from March indicated an improved performance.

Lion bought the brewing assets of the now defunct Bond Corp -- an enterprise four or five times the size of Lion at that time -- in a two-stage deal in 1990. It went on to spend between NZ$200-300 million on upgrading its Australian breweries.
Cairns said the Australian operations had progressed "at the appropriate speed, with a much better balance between the centre and the operational side".
The prospect of supermarket sales of beer under revamped New Zealand liquor laws could stimulate consumption, Lion said.
As a big player in off licence sales, the company said it would see how any change pans out over the next two years before it makes any decision about disposing of its retail operations.

While it has long said that it is not interested in retailing, Lion has remained in the industry for competitive reasons - its main New Zealand market competitor, DB Group Ltd, is also heavily involved in retailing.
Warren Doak at brokers Merrill Lynch said the result was at the top end of expectations, but market share concerns remained.
In New Zealand total sales volumes were down significantly -- six percent -- but market share was steady at 54.4 percent.
As expected, soft drinks and Lion's Chinese operations returned losses of over NZ$5.0 million each.
By 12.15 p.m. (0015 GMT) the company's share price was down nine cents at NZ$3.39 on light volume. (US$1 = NZ$1.44)
